newsitem.title: IRAN: Nateq-Nouri concedes defeat to Khatami in Iran poll.
newsitem.headline: Nateq-Nouri concedes defeat to Khatami in Iran poll.

text.p: Conservative parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri on Saturday conceded defeat to moderate former culture minister Mohammad Khatami in Iran's presidential election, Tehran radio said.

It said Nateq-Nouri sent a message congratulating Khatami on his victory in the most fiercely contested Iranian elections, held to replace President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, since the 1979 Islamic revolution.
Tehran radio quoted an Interior Ministry official as saying Khatami had won 11,713,679 votes so far and Nateq-Nouri had 4,964,866. Some 33 million Iranians aged 15 and older were eligible to vote.
The two other candidates -- Reza Zavarei and Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshari -- had won a total of less than 900,000 votes, the official said.
He said he expected the count to be completed by the end of Saturday.
Analysts had said earlier that if the trend continued, the result would be the biggest political upset in the history of Iran's 18-year-old revolution.
A candidate must win half of all votes to win in the first round.
Both Khatami and Nateq-Nouri are 54-year-old middle-ranking clergymen.

Nateq-Nouri is a traditionalist backed by influential conservative clerics and merchants. He was considered the establishment candidate and was expected to be stronger in rural areas, where vote counting was likely to take longer.

Alireza Tabesh, the official in charge of the election, said the turnout in Friday's ballot was "unprecedentedly heavy". Polling was extended for four extra hours because of queues of people waiting to vote.
Rafsanjani must step down in August after serving the maximum two four-year terms allowed by law.
Khatami's campaign was backed by centrists close to Rafsanjani and Islamist left-wingers who have moderated many of their views in recent years.
The unlikely coalition was formed to counter conservatives which Khatami's backers accused of trying to monopolise state power by adding the presidency to their control of parliament.

Khatami owes his appeal to a reputation as an open-minded religious intellectual and tolerant politician. He gained wide support among women, young people and intellectuals who fear a harder application of Islamic rules in everyday life and restrictions on freedom of expression.

Khatami has advocated more personal freedom, democracy and the rule of law in a country where many complain that state bodies act arbitrarily and rules change according to officials' personal preferences.
Khatami appears to have also drawn many votes from devout Iranians because he holds the title of Seyyed as someone believed to be a descendant of Islam's founder Prophet Mohammad.

All four candidates were screened by a conservative group of senior clergy and lawyers before being allowed to run. The group rejected 234 other candidates for failing to match up to Islamic revolutionary ideals.

Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who outranks the president, tacitly supported Nateq-Nouri. He said voters should choose someone who could "stand against America and those who want to impose their will on our nation".
